page_title: How Big Tech Runs Tech Projects and the Curious Absence of Scrum

sources.entry: How Big Tech Runs Tech Projects and the Curious Absence of Scrum - Gergely Orosz

summary.title: How Big Tech Runs Tech Projects and the Curious Absence of Scrum
summary.one_liner: Big Tech teams usually skip dedicated project managers and Scrum, relying on empowered engineers, TPMs for cross-team work, and strong tooling instead.
keywords: why big tech doesn't use scrum
takeaways: Most Big Tech teams are free to pick their own methodology, often an RFC-like process or Kanban, and rarely use dedicated project managers for team-level work.
Technical Program Managers handle large multi-team projects, while engineers typically lead team-level projects, sometimes rotating the lead role.
Strong CI/CD, feature flags, and automated testing reduce the need for Scrum rituals such as sprint demos and PO sign-offs.
Scrum can still help with 'kitchen sink' teams that face many stakeholder interruptions, such as in non-tech companies and early startups.
Project management method matters less than focus, leadership, and autonomy; the author's Skype vs WhatsApp example illustrates this.
summary.summary: The article, by Gergely Orosz in The Pragmatic Engineer, combines a survey of over 100 companies on project management approaches with the author's first-hand experience at Skype and conversations with people at Big Tech companies. It finds that Big Tech generally lets autonomous engineers lead projects without dedicated project managers, uses TPMs for complex multi-team work, and relies on platform tooling for fast iteration. It explains organizational factors such as autonomy, transparency, and generalist engineers that make this possible. It closes with a defense of Scrum for contexts with conflicting stakeholder priorities.
